p.add: If I mayLet me assume to give a verdict or passingmomentous judgment‸on this poet for the United States—a removed or distant position giving some advantages over a near one.

body.p:
Alfred Tennyson's is a magnificent superb character, and givwillhelps to give illustriousness ‸through the through the long roll of time to theour Nineteenth Century. In its gr bunch of greatorbic names, shining like a constellation of stars, his will remain one of the brightest. His very fears,‸faults, doubts, swervings, ‸doublings upon himself, have been are typical of the timeof our age. We are like the voyagers of a ship casting off for new lines, new waters,seas and distant shores; we ‸would still dwell onin the old ‸suffocating and dead haunts, remembering‸and magnify their goodpleasant ex-
periencesexperiences only, and are, more more than once impelled to jump ashore‸before it is too late and stay where our fathers staid, and live as they did.
To me, Tennyson shows, more than any one I know, new, or old, how much there is in verbalism.

There is a ‸latent charm in mere certaincunning words, ‸collocations, and in the voice ringing them, which he has caught, and sometimes renders,brought out, beyond all other men, in some of his lines:
"And hollow, hollow, hollow, all delight," in "the Passing of Arthur,"; and all through, ashis pieces, evidenced in "the Deserted House" and "the Lady of Shalott."

‸His mannerism is great, but it is a good and noble mannerism.. His ‸very best work, is to me, is contained in the books of the "Idylls of the King," all of them, and all that has grown out of them, including. Indeed‸Though indeed we can spare nothing of Tennyson, however small or peculiar—"Flower in the Crannied Wall" or "Lady Clare" or Among the best, (I often linger over them again and again) are "Lucretius," ‸"the Lotos Eaters" and "the Northern Farmer"
May⹀be I am non⹀literary and non⹀conventional, ‸(let me at least be human, and pay part of my debt) in this effusionword about Tennyson

I want him to know that here is a great‸and ardent nation who absorbs his words,songs, and respects him and has an affection for him, ‸personally, as almost for no other foreigner, I want these wordsthis word to go to the old man, at Farringford, as a balmy breath something to solace the life—for they tell no more than the simple truth—and the truth, the gift they convey is no small one
